recipe.history:
Cheese is one of the oldest preserved foods in human history, with evidence of cheesemaking dating back at least seven thousand years to Neolithic Poland, where pottery fragments have been found bearing traces of milk fat consistent with cheese straining. The practice of making cheese from the milk of domesticated animals — cattle, sheep, and goats — emerged independently across multiple cultures in the ancient Near East, Europe, and Central Asia, driven by the universal need to preserve milk in an era before refrigeration. Each of the five cheeses in this burger represents a distinct cheesemaking tradition and culture: cheddar originates in the caves and cellars of Cheddar Gorge in Somerset, England, where the cool, humid air creates the conditions for aging that produce its characteristic sharp, crumbly quality; Gruyère comes from the Swiss canton of Fribourg, where it has been made since the twelfth century in large copper vats from the rich milk of cows grazing high Alpine meadows; mozzarella traces its origins to the Campania region of southern Italy, traditionally made from water buffalo milk in the area around Naples; Brie, known as the queen of French cheeses, comes from the Seine-et-Marne region east of Paris, where the bloomy-rind soft ripened cheese was served at the royal court by the ninth century; and Parmigiano-Reggiano, the king of Italian cheeses, has been produced in the Po Valley of northern Italy under strict geographical and methodological regulations for nearly a thousand years.

Five-cheese burgers are a tradition born from excess and ambition — the American tendency to ask not why but why not when it comes to stacking flavors. The cheeseburger itself became standardized in American culture in the 1930s, first appearing on menus in California and the Midwest almost simultaneously, and within decades the single slice of American cheese had given way to double cheese, triple cheese, and cheese blends as restaurants competed for distinction. The artisan burger movement of the early twenty-first century brought European and farmstead cheeses onto burger menus, where their complex flavors, different melting behaviors, and varied textures created new possibilities. Layering five cheeses — each one placed at a different structural level in the burger — creates a composition in which each bite passes through a different cheesy experience: the aged sharpness of cheddar at the base, the nutty melt of Gruyère, the fresh pull of mozzarella, the cool cream of Brie, the salty granular punch of Parmesan at the top.

The five-cheese composition in this burger was born from a Thursday afternoon when I had a nearly empty refrigerator and a well-stocked cheese drawer and a deep reluctance to go to the store. I had half a block of sharp cheddar, the end of a Gruyère wedge, some fresh mozzarella I had bought for a salad, a ripe Brie that was threatening to overflow its rind, and a heel of Parmigiano that I had been grating over pasta for weeks. I laid them all out on the counter and looked at them and thought: every one of these is good. Every one of these would be good on a burger. And then I thought: what if they were all on the same burger? The experiment was not subtle, but it was magnificent, and the version I have refined since that afternoon is the burger I am most proud of, because it proves that the answer to how much cheese is always more.

Five cheeses on one burger create an environment of extraordinary richness. The only beef that can hold its own in this company is a medium-rare patty cooked to 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — pink, yielding, fat-rich, and still expressing its own character rather than acting as a neutral bun for cheese to sit on. A well-done patty under five cheeses becomes invisible — it is dry protein surrounded by molten fat from all sides, a meat sponge soaked in cheese rather than a participant in the flavor conversation. Medium rare keeps the beef present, keeps the juices in the meat, keeps every bite a negotiation between the patty's iron-rich beefiness and the accumulated cheese wealth above it. Cook it right. Five cheeses deserve the best beef you can give them.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 slice sharp aged cheddar (layer 1 — on the patty)
1 slice Gruyère (layer 2 — melted over the cheddar)
1 slice fresh mozzarella, 1/4-inch thick (layer 3 — on top of Gruyère)
1 oz ripe Brie, rind removed, at room temperature (layer 4 — spread on bottom bun)
1 tbsp freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano (layer 5 — sprinkled on top bun)
2 cloves garlic, minced and mashed to a paste
4 large shallots, peeled and thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Combine warm milk, warm water, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Add flour one cup at a time with the dough hook on low until a shaggy dough forms. Increase to medium speed, add butter cube by cube, and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth, elastic, and glossy. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate 8 hours or overnight.

2. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape into tight balls. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover loosely, and proof at room temperature 1.5 to 2 hours. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

3. Make the garlic herb butter: Combine softened butter, garlic paste, parsley, thyme, lemon zest, and salt in a small bowl. Mix until uniformly combined. Refrigerate until firm, then slice into pats for use during cooking and bun toasting.

4. Make the caramelized shallots: Heat butter and olive oil in a small skillet over medium-low heat. Add shallot rings and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 25 to 30 minutes until deeply golden and sweet. Add sugar and balsamic vinegar in the last 5 minutes. Cook until liquid evaporates. Set aside.
5. Prepare the Brie: Remove rind from Brie portions. Let the Brie sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes so it becomes spreadable.

6. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions. Form into 4-inch patties, 3/4-inch thick, with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

7. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat. Lightly oil the surface. Sear patties dimple-side up, undisturbed, for 3 minutes. Flip once. Immediately place a slice of sharp cheddar on each patty. After 60 seconds, lay a slice of Gruyère on top of the cheddar. After another 60 seconds, place a slice of fresh mozzarella on top of the Gruyère. Cover the skillet with a lid or aluminum foil tent and cook until internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F and the cheeses are melted and layered. Remove from heat and tent loosely with foil. Rest 3 minutes.

8. While patties rest, split buns and toast cut-side down in garlic herb butter in the skillet over medium heat until golden, fragrant, and glistening, about 90 seconds. While buns toast, grate Parmigiano-Reggiano over each top bun's cut side so the heat of the bun slightly softens it.
9. Toss arugula with lemon juice, olive oil, and a pinch of salt.

10. Assemble the burgers: Spread softened Brie generously and evenly over the bottom bun's cut surface (layer 4 — the Brie melts slightly on the warm bun). Place a small handful of arugula on top of the Brie. Lay the caramelized shallots on the arugula. Place the rested patty with its three melted cheeses on top. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt over the cheese stack. Close with the Parmigiano-dusted top bun. Serve immediately.
